paper_sections.title: Damaged Insula Network Contributes to Depression in Parkinson’s Disease

description.value: The study investigated insula functional connectivity abnormalities in Parkinson’s disease and examined depression-related connectivity changes in depressed versus non-depressed patients.

design.value: Two groups of PD patients, with and without depression, and a group of age- and sex-matched normal controls underwent resting-state BOLD fMRI. Seed-based functional connectivity maps from bilateral anterior and posterior insula regions were compared across groups, with age and sex used as covariates.

description.value: Scores of the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale were obtained from all subjects.
Scores of the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression were obtained from all subjects.
Scores of the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale were obtained from all subjects.
Scores of the Mini-Mental State Examination were obtained from all subjects.

source_definition.value: The three groups were depressed PD patients, non-depressed PD patients, and normal controls.
Age was used as a covariate in the general linear models.
Sex was used as a covariate in the general linear models.
FC between left anterior insula and left MFG showed significant correlation with MMSE scores.

inclusion_criteria.value: The PD diagnosis was made by a senior neurologist according to the UK PD Brain Bank criteria.
Unipolar depression was diagnosed by an experienced psychiatrist according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition criteria (DSM-IV).

exclusion_criteria.value: Cerebrovascular disorders, including a previous stroke, a history of seizure, hydrocephalus, an intracranial mass, a history of head injury, previous neurological surgery, or other neurological diseases.
Any current DSM-IV Axis I diagnosis other than MDD.
Treatment with antidepressants or other psychiatric therapy.
Participants who were unable to keep still during the MRI because of head motion.

task_description.value: Subjects were instructed to relax with their eyes closed without falling asleep, and without directed systematic thought.

instructions.value: Relax with their eyes closed without falling asleep, and without directed systematic thought.

description.value: Blood oxygenation level dependent images were acquired using an echo planar imaging sequence. TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 90°, FOV = 240 × 240 mm², matrix = 64 × 64, slice thickness = 5 mm, slice gap = 1 mm, 23 interleaved axial slices. A total of 185 resting-state BOLD images were acquired from each subject.
A 3-D GRE T1-weighted sequence was acquired after functional imaging. TR/TE = 5.14 ms/1.17 ms, FOV = 240 × 240 mm², matrix = 256 × 256, slice thickness = 1.2 mm, no gap, 124 sagittal slices.

The first 10 images were excluded; remaining images were slice-time corrected, realigned, nuisance-regressed, normalized into standard space using DARTEL, resampled to 3 × 3 × 3 mm, smoothed with a 6-mm Gaussian kernel, detrended, and bandpass filtered at 0.01~0.1 Hz. Framewise displacement scrubbing excluded time points with FD > 0.5 mm; subjects with fewer than 130 remaining time points were excluded.

software.value: Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI (DPARSF)
Resting-State fMRI Data Analysis Toolkit (REST V1.8)

steps.value: The first 10 images were excluded from the analysis.
Slice timing was corrected using the middle slice as a reference.
Images were realigned to remove head motion.
Friston-24 head motion parameters and white matter and CSF signals calculated using the CompCor method were regressed out.
Images were normalized into standard space using DARTEL and resampled to 3 × 3 × 3 mm voxel size.
Images were smoothed using a 6-mm Gaussian kernel.
Bandpass filtering was performed at 0.01~0.1 Hz.
Subjects having head motion with >2 mm of translation or 2° of rotation were excluded.
Time points where FD > 0.5 mm were censored; subjects whose total length of data were <130 were excluded.

model_settings.value: Pearson’s correlation was calculated between the average time series within the ROIs and other brain areas. The resulting connectivity maps were transformed to Z maps using Fisher r-to-z transformation. Age and sex were used as covariates.

estimator.value: Pearson’s correlation; Fisher r-to-z transformation; one-sample and general linear model comparisons
